title: Airport transit availability is not the same as practical mobility
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office GAO-26-107817; airport public-transit availability, passenger and employee use, and transportation-demand management
geography: United States commercial airports; all 31 large-hub airports and selected medium/small airports, plus Census employee-commute estimates

observations.period: 2025–2026 airport review; 51 airports including all 31 large hubs and 20 selected medium/small hubs

denominator.unit: airports reviewed; all 31 large-hub airports plus a random selection of 20 medium- and small-hub airports

any_transit_service.value: all but two small airports reviewed had some bus or rail service

large_airport_rail.unit: of 31 large airports with rail service; 18 connected on airport grounds or by dedicated air-train and 5 by free bus from off-site rail

medium_small_service.value: the 20 selected medium and small airports generally had bus service between the airport curb and local downtown

observations.method: GAO review of airport websites and documentation, confirmation contacts with all 51 airports, literature review, and interviews with DOT and stakeholder organizations.
observations.uncertainty: The 51-airport design is not a complete census of every commercial airport or trip; some service does not establish frequency, span, fare, reliability, directness, accessibility, residential reach, or shift fit.
observations.subgroup: Large-hub airports and selected medium/small-hub airports under the stated FAA 2023 enplanement frame.
observations.counterinterpretation: A route may be practically useful for a subset of passengers or workers even when it is not suitable for early shifts, dispersed origins, mobility-aid needs, or unfamiliar riders; low uptake is not by itself service failure.

observations.period: 2019–2023 Census commute data and airport reports reviewed in 2025–2026; transit use

denominator.unit: airports with usable passenger mode reports; separate from two visited-airport employee surveys and national Census employee estimates

passenger_transit_use_range.unit: public-transit share across the 12 airports with passenger mode reports

visited_employee_transit_use.unit: public-transit share among surveyed employees at two large airports

national_airport_airline_employee_transi.unit: percent estimated to use public transit to commute, based on GAO Census analysis

observations.method: GAO synthesis of airport passenger mode reports, two visited-airport employee surveys, and 2019–2023 Census commute analysis.
observations.uncertainty: These figures use different universes, designs, reporting methods, and geographies; they are not a national ridership average, causal comparison, or measure of completed trips, missed work, household cost, or worker choice.
observations.subgroup: Passengers at 12 airports with usable reports, employees at two visited large airports, and national airport/airline employees in Census commute data.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher use at a local airport can reflect better service, residential geography, parking cost, workforce composition, or fewer alternatives; lower use can reflect preference, unfamiliarity, shift timing, or service mismatch.

observations.period: 2025–2026; factors affecting transit decisions and transportation-demand management

denominator.unit: airports GAO visited that were implementing transportation-demand-management strategies

decision_factors.value: cost, travel time, familiarity, elevator or mobility-aid accommodation, parking, transit benefits, and work-shift matching

tdm_strategies.value: signage, advertising, reduced-cost or free transit, and related promotion/incentive efforts

goal_measurement.unit: visited airports that set or planned to assess transit-use goals

observations.method: GAO interviews and review of airport/transit-agency transportation-demand-management strategies and plans.
observations.uncertainty: An intervention or stated goal is not increased ridership, dependable trip completion, lower congestion, reduced emissions, lower household cost, or improved labor access; distributional effects and intervention timing remain unmeasured.
observations.subgroup: Passengers, airport and airline employees, airports, transit agencies, and workers with early/overnight shifts or mobility-access needs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Promotion may improve discoverability for riders who already have a workable route while leaving those with inaccessible, costly, or shift-incompatible service dependent on private vehicles.

related_sources.claim: Official GAO review supplies airport availability, passenger and employee use, decision factors, TDM strategies, methods, and measurement limits.

boundary: This record establishes airport transit supply, use, and demand-management stages beneath practical mobility. It does not establish route-level accessibility, completed trips, missed work, household transport cost, airport labor supply, congestion, emissions, intervention effects, trust, or political response.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO HTML report page retrieved and hashed; report PDF, Census microdata, transit schedules, and airport administrative files not retained
